breadcrumb.name: Watts to Amps Calculator for DC, Single-Phase and Three-Phase

p: On a 230 V home supply, 1,500 W is 6.52 A for a heater, kettle or iron (power factor one) and 8.15 A for a motor or AC at a power factor of 0.8. The watts are the same; the motor draws more current because part of it flows back and forth without doing work.
On a 120 V US supply the same heater draws 12.5 A, close to twice as much current, so always enter the voltage of the supply the load actually runs on.

sections.h2: Is 1,000 watts one amp? How many watts per amp?
p: No. A watt is power, an amp is current, and the voltage links them. 1,000 W is 83.33 A from a 12 V battery but 4.35 A from 230 V mains. The higher the voltage, the fewer amps for the same watts.
Each amp carries as many watts as the voltage times the power factor: on 230 V mains with a power factor of one, one amp is 230 W. The amps to watts calculator does that direction.

sections.h2: Watts, amps and volts: how they relate
p: Power is voltage times current. On DC that is the whole story: watts = volts × amps. On AC the current and voltage are slightly out of step in motors, compressors and electronics, so a power factor below one is added: watts = volts × amps × power factor.

Three-phase supplies use three live wires. The power is shared between them, so the formula uses the square root of three and the line-to-line voltage (400 V in Pakistan), and the result is the current in each line.

sections.h2: DC watts to amps: batteries, solar and cars
p: Choose DC and enter the battery voltage. A 1,000 W load on a 12 V battery draws 83.33 A, which is why low-voltage inverters need thick cables. On a battery inverter, add the inverter's losses to the watts first; the 12V watts to amps calculator does this for you.

faq.a: 4.35 A on a 230 V single-phase supply with a power factor of one. From a 12 V battery the same 1,000 W draws 83.33 A, because current depends on the voltage.
6.52 A at 230 V for a heating load, and 8.15 A at a power factor of 0.8 for a motor or mixed load.

faq.q: How many amps does a 1,500 W heater draw at 120 V?
faq.a: 12.5 A at 120 V, against 6.52 A on a 230 V supply. Roughly halving the voltage roughly doubles the current, which is why US heaters need heavier cable.

faq.q: What is the watts to amps formula?
faq.a: Amps = watts ÷ volts for DC; amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor) for single-phase AC; amps = watts ÷ (√3 × line-to-line volts × power factor) for three-phase.
No. Watts measure power and amps measure current. 1,000 W is 4.35 A on 230 V mains and 83.33 A from a 12 V battery.
Watts per amp equals the voltage times the power factor. On 230 V mains with a power factor of one, each amp carries 230 W; on a 12 V battery each amp carries only 12 W.

faq.q: How do I convert watts to amps on three-phase?
faq.a: Divide the watts by √3 × the line-to-line voltage × the power factor. 10,000 W at 400 V and a power factor of 0.8 is 18.04 A per line. The 3 phase amps calculator also handles kW and kVA ratings.

key_facts: Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). On a 230 V single-phase supply, 1,500 W at a power factor of 0.8 draws 8.15 A.
Watts alone do not give amps: the same 1,000 W draws 83.33 A from a 12 V battery but only 4.35 A at 230 V mains with a power factor of one.
At 120 V (US and Canada) a 1,500 W heater draws 12.5 A, close to twice the 6.52 A the same heater draws on a 230 V supply.
On three-phase 400 V, 10,000 W at a power factor of 0.8 draws 18.04 A in each line wire.
mistakes: Dividing watts by volts for an AC, fridge or water motor. Their power factor is below one, so the real current is higher; use about 0.8 unless the label says otherwise.
Using 230 V in the three-phase formula. Three-phase needs the line-to-line voltage (400 V) together with the square root of three.
Forgetting that DC current is large at low voltage. A load that draws a few amps from the mains can draw tens of amps from a battery, and the cable must be sized for that.
Treating the calculated amps as the breaker or wire size. Cables and breakers need a margin above the running current; the breaker size calculator adds it.

sources.label: IEC 60038:2009, IEC standard voltages (230/400 V, 120/240 V systems)
NEPRA, National Electric Power Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (supply standards: 230 V single-phase, 400 V three-phase, 50 Hz)

how.tpl: {{in.watts}} W ÷ ({{out.k|4}} × {{out.volts}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor) = {{out.amps|2}} A. The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are the line-to-line voltage and the result is the current in each line. On DC the power factor is always one, so amps are simply watts ÷ volts.
how.text: 1,500 W ÷ (1 × 230 V × 0.8 power factor) = 8.15 A. The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are the line-to-line voltage and the result is the current in each line. On DC the power factor is always one, so amps are simply watts ÷ volts.

examples.title: What is 1,500 W in amps on a 230 V supply?
examples.text: 1,500 W ÷ (230 V × 1) = 6.52 A for a heater or kettle. A motor of the same watts at a power factor below one draws more.

examples.title: 1,000 W from a 12 V battery (DC)
examples.text: 1,000 W ÷ 12 V = 83.33 A. DC has no power factor, so this is the current the battery and its cable must carry, before inverter losses.

examples.title: 10,000 W on three-phase 400 V
examples.text: 10,000 W ÷ (√3 × 400 V × 0.8) = 18.04 A in each line. The voltage box was left blank, so the calculator used the standard three-phase line-to-line voltage.

examples.title: 1,500 W heater at 120 V (US and Canada)
examples.text: 1,500 W ÷ (120 V × 1) = 12.5 A. A lower voltage means more amps for the same watts.

examples.title: How many amps is 1,000 watts at 230 V?
examples.text: 1,000 W ÷ (230 V × 1) = 4.35 A for a resistive load such as an iron or water heater.

content.answer: 1,500 watts is 8.15 amps on a 230 V single-phase supply at a power factor of 0.8, or 6.52 A for a heater with a power factor of one. Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor); for DC the power factor is one, and for three-phase the volts are multiplied by the square root of three.

formula.text: DC: I = P ÷ V;  single-phase AC: I = P ÷ (V × PF);  three-phase AC: I = P ÷ (√3 × V × PF)
lines: P = real power in watts (W); for kW multiply by 1,000
V = voltage: the battery voltage for DC, phase-to-neutral for single-phase, line-to-line for three-phase
PF = power factor between 0 and 1 (1 for heating loads)

content.safety: The current from this page is a starting point for choosing cable and breakers, not the final choice. Use the wire size and breaker size calculators for the margins and voltage drop, and have a licensed electrician connect any new circuit.
